Done

Yes, iron deficiency is associated with an increased risk of seizures, particularly febrile seizures in children. The relationship with afebrile seizures and epilepsy in adults is less well established.

Febrile Seizures in Children

The strongest evidence links iron deficiency to febrile seizures in children under age 5. Multiple meta-analyses support this association:

  • A 2023 meta-analysis of 20 case-control studies (3,856 participants) found that iron deficiency anemia, low MCV, low serum iron, high TIBC, and low ferritin were all associated with increased febrile seizure risk, with odds ratios ranging from 1.24 to 1.59. Low serum ferritin had the highest diagnostic accuracy among iron indices. Child Neurology[1]

  • An earlier meta-analysis of 17 studies (4,803 children) found iron deficiency anemia was significantly associated with febrile seizures (OR 1.98, 95% CI 1.26–3.13), with the strongest association when diagnosed by low ferritin (OR 3.78, 95% CI 1.80–7.94). Seizure[2]

  • A prospective case-control study from South Korea found ferritin <30 ng/mL carried an OR of 6.18 (95% CI 2.32–16.42) for febrile seizures, suggesting that iron deficiency even prior to overt anemia may increase risk. BMC Pediatrics[3]

Notably, iron deficiency does not appear to increase the risk of all acute seizure types equally — a meta-analysis found the association was specific to febrile seizures rather than acute seizures in general. PloS One[4]

Iron and Epilepsy

The relationship between iron and epilepsy is more complex. Abnormal iron metabolism — including both deficiency and overload — has been implicated in epilepsy susceptibility. Frontiers in Cell and Developmental Biology[5] Iron overload and ferroptosis (iron-dependent cell death via lipid peroxidation) are associated with post-stroke and post-traumatic epilepsy. Frontiers in Neuroscience[6] However, the evidence for iron deficiency as a direct cause of afebrile epileptic seizures in adults remains limited and largely preclinical.

Proposed Mechanisms

Iron plays a critical role in neurotransmitter synthesis (including GABA and monoamines), myelination, and neuronal energy metabolism. Iron deficiency may lower the seizure threshold by impairing these processes, particularly in the developing brain. Some authors have recommended routine iron status screening in children presenting with febrile seizures and consideration of iron supplementation in those found to be deficient. Pediatric Hematology/Oncology + 1[7-8]

Would you like to explore whether iron supplementation has been shown to reduce febrile seizure recurrence in iron-deficient children?
